video_title: Time To Start Getting REALLY Bullish? | Tom McClellan
gist: Technician Tom McClellan says the market is in the final week or so of a seasonal presidential-cycle bottom and expects to flip aggressively bullish into a third-year advance, with record margin debt not becoming a problem until a ~7-year cycle top around 2028; he is bearish bonds and bullish oil because gold leads both long-term yields and crude by roughly 20 months, pointing to an Aug-2028 peak. New Harbor Financial's Mike Preston and John Lodra, reacting to the same day's surprise unanimous 25bp Fed rate HIKE (first since July 2023), agree on the cycle read but are tactically bullish high-quality bonds and warn that averaged cycle charts hide lost-decade outliers.

insights.claim: Tom McClellan says US equities are in the squishy seasonal bottoming zone of the presidential cycle and he expects the final low within about a week, after which he intends to turn aggressively bullish for the next 12 months.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Sets a dated, falsifiable re-entry window: adding risk into the late-September/early-October washout rather than waiting for confirmation is the trade he is telegraphing.
insights.quote: I am not bullish today, but I am looking for the moment probably within the next week to turn bullish and then I'm going to be bullish as all get out.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is running roughly a week AHEAD of the normal presidential-cycle seasonal schedule, so the usual bottoming turns are arriving early and waiting for the textbook calendar date risks missing the launch.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Argues for front-running the seasonal low by days rather than waiting for the classic mid-October date.

insights.claim: The third year of a US presidential term has been up essentially every time since the 20th Amendment changed the political calendar, with only 1931 (Great Depression) and 1939 (Wehrmacht invading Poland) as exceptions.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: A base rate that argues against shorting or de-risking into 2027 absent a depression- or world-war-scale shock.

insights.claim: The pre-midterm stock market bottom arrives about a month BEFORE the election because investors price the certainty of having an outcome, not the outcome itself — so the partisan result of the 2026 midterms should not drive positioning.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Removes election-result handicapping as an input; buy the pre-election certainty bid instead of waiting for results.
insights.quote: the actual outcome of the election matters way far less than the certainty of knowing that we have an out an outcome

insights.claim: McClellan's checklist for flipping bullish is a day with a high put/call ratio, a high VIX, and breadth divergences — specifically a higher low in the McClellan Oscillator against a lower price low.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: A concrete, monitorable trigger set for timing the entry rather than a vague 'buy the dip'.

insights.claim: The 10-year decennial pattern applied to the Dow also points to a bottom in early October, with years ending in seven bullish in their first half starting from October — 1987 was a late-in-the-year exception, not an early-year one.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: A second, independent seasonal model corroborating the same October inflection and a bullish first half of 2027.

insights.claim: Averaged cycle patterns reliably reproduce the timing of market turns (the 'dance steps') but not the slope, and exogenous shocks such as the Iran war or the Strait of Hormuz reopening distort the slope while leaving the turn dates intact.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Tells you how to use seasonal composites: trade the timing of inflections, never the implied price target.

insights.claim: Because only a handful of presidential cycles exist since the 1930s calendar change, squeezing nuanced sub-forecasts out of the composite (e.g. that current above-average strength borrows from next year) runs into sample-size trouble.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Guards against over-fitting seasonal data; use the pattern directionally, not for magnitude adjustments.

insights.claim: McClellan's structural bull case is fiscal: Americans are not being taxed to the hilt, so more money stays in the private economy to be spent and to build factories, which is bullish for stocks even while it creates problems for the government.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Frames low federal tax-to-GDP as a persistent equity tailwind — and any tax-raising turn as the bearish signpost to watch.

insights.claim: Deficit spending is an explicitly bullish factor for stocks in McClellan's framework, and a Congress that reined in spending toward a balanced budget would be a big bearish factor because it would remove liquidity that lifts stock prices.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual fiscal-hawk read: fiscal discipline, not profligacy, is the equity risk event to watch for.

themes.theme: Breadth strength vs. high-yield credit divergence

insights.claim: The NYSE advance-decline line has been making tops alongside price tops with no bearish divergence, which McClellan reads as ample liquidity reaching even the lowly stocks and a bullish condition for the broad market.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Absence of a breadth divergence removes the classic pre-top warning, supporting staying long into the seasonal turn.

insights.claim: In McClellan's long-running study, after a new three-year high in the NYSE advance-decline line the worst-case drawdown over the following three months is about 10%, with the average nearer 4%; the exceptions were COVID and the abrupt endings of QE1 and QE2.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Quantifies downside risk after a breadth thrust — roughly a 10% worst case unless the Fed abruptly yanks liquidity or a pandemic-scale shock hits.

insights.claim: The one bearish thorn in McClellan's case is the corporate high-yield bond advance-decline line, which has diverged from high-yield prices for all of 2026 — a divergence he keeps waiting to matter and that has not yet mattered the way the 2022 version did.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: The single indicator that would invalidate the bullish setup; watch junk-bond breadth for resolution rather than price alone.

insights.claim: Corporate high-yield bonds are far more sensitive to stock-market liquidity than to the level of interest rates, so blaming their 2026 weakness on rising yields and refinancing at higher rates is the wrong causal model.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Makes junk-bond action a liquidity gauge for equities rather than a rates trade — and means falling yields alone will not fix it.
insights.quote: they're way more sensitive to the stock market liquidity than they are to what other interest rates are doing

insights.claim: McClellan frames junk bonds as intrinsically bad investments that only perform when so much money is sloshing around that even the crappy assets get some, making them the first place liquidity stress shows up.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Use high-yield performance as the leading tell on systemic liquidity before it reaches equities.
insights.quote: These are horrible investments. Corporate high yield bonds. They're junk bonds.

insights.claim: The McClellan Oscillator built on the high-yield advance-decline line is at an extreme low, which McClellan reads as the worst of the selling being wrung out, with the final price low likely within about a week since the breadth low typically precedes the price low.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Gives a specific sequencing test: breadth low first, price low within days — a failure of that sequence would break the bull case.

insights.claim: McClellan's named confirming signal for the October-November rally is junk bonds starting to outperform, which would say there is so much money around that even the crappy investments can do well.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: A tradeable confirmation trigger — high-yield credit turning up validates adding equity risk.

themes.theme: Record margin debt and the seven-year top cycle

insights.claim: FINRA margin debt is at a record and even normalized by GDP is higher than anything in the series back to 1997, and such peaks coincide with — and typically occur slightly before — important stock market tops.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Confirms the leverage risk is real but positions margin debt as a leading top indicator to be watched for its peak, not its level.

insights.claim: Peaks in margin debt relative to GDP recur on a roughly seven-year cycle, and counting forward from the last peak in August 2021 puts the next one around 2028 — which is why McClellan does not treat today's record leverage as a sell signal.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Turns the most-cited bearish datapoint into a permission slip for another 18 months of upside, with 2028 as the risk date.
insights.quote: five is not seven and we are five years from from the the peak the last of these peaks

insights.claim: The same seven-year top cycle shows up in the St. Louis Fed's quarterly margin data going back to 1945, though at roughly 'seven-ish' rather than exactly 7.0 years, making it useful for windows rather than precise dates.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Longer history strengthens the cycle claim while capping how precisely it can be traded.

insights.claim: McClellan attributes the seven-year cycle not to anything planetary but to a human behavioral rhythm — investors get frenzied at tops, get discouraged, and take about seven years to work up to frenzy again.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: A behavioral rather than mechanical rationale, which means the cycle can stretch and should not be traded to the month.

insights.claim: McClellan sees three cycles converging on 2028 — the seven-year margin-debt and stock-market top, the peak in crude oil, and the peak in interest rates — implying whoever wins the 2028 presidential election inherits a margin-debt collapse in their first year, 2029.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Defines the horizon for the bull case: be positioned aggressively into 2027, defensively approaching 2028.

insights.claim: Rising consumer use of buy-now-pay-later for everyday purchases is framed by McClellan as part of the same leverage build-out as record margin debt, which keeps increasing until it reaches a breaking point he dates to 2028.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Links consumer credit expansion to the same cycle clock, suggesting consumer-lender stress arrives on the same 2028 timeline.

themes.theme: QE5, stealth balance-sheet tightening, and the bond paradox

insights.claim: McClellan counts the current Fed regime as QE5 and says that since Warsh took over the slope of balance-sheet expansion has quietly flattened — MBS is being sold while Treasuries are bought — with no announcement and a further slowdown in the latest data.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: The liquidity impulse is fading without a policy announcement — track the weekly H.4.1 balance sheet rather than the press conference.
insights.quote: this is one of the reasons you got to not just watch the press conference, you got to look at the data

insights.claim: The single identified way the bullish setup gets ruined is the Fed shifting to full-blown quantitative tightening and pulling money out of the banking system — something not mentioned at the latest FOMC announcement but visible in the data.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Names the specific invalidator for the bull thesis, making Fed balance-sheet data the key risk monitor.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart notes Warsh said during his consideration as Fed chair that he does not plan to monkey around with the balance sheet and thinks it should be lowered over time while using interest rates as the main policy tool — consistent with a quiet slowdown in asset purchases.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Supports expecting continued stealth balance-sheet shrinkage alongside rate-based policy, a headwind for liquidity-sensitive assets.

insights.claim: Every round of QE has coincided with falling bond prices — 2009's QE1, 2011's QE2, QE3 in 2012-13, QE4 after COVID and now QE5 — the opposite of the intuitive demand effect, and bonds went sideways only when QE stopped.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Implies a shift to QT would be a bullish mitigant for bonds, and that ongoing QE is a reason to stay short duration.
insights.quote: at some point, you got to stop arguing with how it should work and realize how it does work

insights.claim: The Fed raised the federal funds rate by 25bp — the first increase since July 2023 — on a unanimous 12-0 vote, which was itself the surprise after recent meetings were marked by dissent, with messaging pointing to at least one more hike this year.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: A unanimous hiking committee removes the 'Warsh was brought in to cut' narrative and repriceses the front end higher.

insights.claim: CME FedWatch for the December 2026 meeting showed zero probability of cuts and about an 88% probability of further hikes — roughly 48% for one more 25bp and nearly 40% for two — an almost exact inversion of expectations a year ago.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Market-implied path is now one-sided toward hikes, which raises the payoff to any dovish surprise and pressures rate-sensitive assets.

insights.claim: The market's reaction to the hike was an initial spike higher that reversed during the press conference, with the S&P closing down just under half a percent, precious metals and commodities selling off hard, and long-term Treasuries among the few assets closing green.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Long bonds catching a bid on a hawkish hike hints at growth-fear positioning rather than inflation panic.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield topped out at 5.016% on the day of the hike, the upper end of a three-plus-year range roughly between 3.2% and 5%, and closed slightly below that level.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: A clean technical level: a decisive break above 5% would confirm McClellan's secular rate-rise thesis and break New Harbor's range trade.

themes.theme: Gold's 20-month lead on yields and oil

insights.claim: Gold prices lead the 30-year Treasury yield by about 20.5 months in McClellan's work, so the violent gold advance of late 2025 into early 2026 implies a steep rise in long-term yields beginning toward the end of this year.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: A dated roadmap for being short duration into 2027 and for hedging rate-sensitive equity exposure.

insights.claim: McClellan is explicit that the gold lead transfers direction and timing of turns but NOT magnitude — gold doubling does not mean yields double — and he says he only needs the direction to know how to position.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Prevents over-extrapolating the model into specific yield targets while still using it for trend direction.

insights.claim: Because gold topped in January 2026, counting forward about 20 months puts the peak in both interest rates and crude oil prices around August 2028.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Gives a specific date to start expecting the rates and energy uptrends to roll over — and a target for extending bond duration.

insights.claim: The same lead relationship maps gold onto crude oil with a 19.8-month offset going back to 2014, and the current oil advance is right on schedule coming out of gold's consolidation, implying crude has a lot further to run until roughly 2028.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Supports a multi-year long-energy stance and a structurally higher fuel-cost assumption for transport and delivery businesses.

insights.claim: The pain from McClellan's projected rise in long-term yields lands mainly in the mortgage market and on home buyers, since corporate expansion and capex are tied much more to short-term rates than to the 10-year and 30-year.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Directs the short toward housing and real-estate-linked exposure rather than broad corporate credit.

insights.claim: McClellan does not dispute a scenario in which the 30-year cracks 6% and the 10-year reaches around 5.5% as yields follow gold's path, calling those numbers reasonable to get to from here.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Puts concrete levels on the bond-bear case that would devastate long-duration portfolios and mortgage affordability.

insights.claim: The main acknowledged weakness in the gold-leads-everything model is that the recent gold surge was driven by central bank buying, especially China, rather than by the normal investor base — which McClellan concedes is a question that keeps him up at night.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: If official-sector demand carries a different information content than private demand, the 2028 rate and oil projections lose their foundation.
insights.quote: That's a that's a question that keeps me up at night and I wish I had a perfect answer.

insights.claim: Commercial traders in crude oil futures — largely producers hedging output — have stayed net short continuously since 2009, and their net short position is now unusually low even with oil back above 100, meaning hedgers are refusing to lock in current prices.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Producer hedging reluctance is a bullish confirmation for crude; a surge back to a high net-short is the signal that the oil top is in.

insights.claim: The practical takeaway from the gold-lead work is that higher-for-longer in both oil and interest rates is the bet to make, with consumer adaptation coming through smaller cars, less driving and fewer delivery orders.
insights.speaker: Tom McClellan
insights.so_what: Favors energy and short-duration positioning while pressuring delivery-dependent and discretionary consumer businesses.

themes.theme: Bond bear thesis vs. New Harbor's cyclical bond trade

insights.claim: New Harbor Financial is fundamentally bullish high-quality US bonds against McClellan's bearish view, arguing sentiment is washed out and that a hard stock-market drop would bring the Fed back to printing and trigger a flight-to-safety rally in rates.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Explicit two-sided debate on duration; the resolution hinges on whether the next shock is a growth scare or an inflation impulse.

insights.claim: Mike Preston sketches TLT trading at 81 and down year to date going to 120 — a roughly 50% gain — if stocks fall hard and the 10-year yield returns to 3.5%, 4% or even 3%, while stressing these are guesses based on charts rather than predictions.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the asymmetric payoff in long-duration Treasuries as a hedge against an equity break.
insights.quote: I could see that going to 120.

insights.claim: New Harbor's bond call is explicitly a two-year cyclical trade, not a buy-and-hold — they expect a good trade in long-term US government bonds over the next couple of years followed by a headwind for the following ten years once the market figures out inflation is a problem.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Reconciles the bull and bear bond views: rent duration for the cyclical rally, do not own it for the secular trend.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart frames the two bond views as compatible — a violent cyclical bond rally can occur inside McClellan's secular uptrend in yields, because the gold-lead model dictates direction over 20 months rather than continuous movement.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Suggests trading bonds tactically while keeping the structural short-duration bias intact.

insights.claim: New Harbor holds about a 32% fixed income allocation with average duration around five years, of which roughly 7.5% of portfolios is in long-term Treasuries, and would extend maturities if technical improvement appears.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Shows the conviction is expressed in modest size — a tactical tilt, not a table-pounding duration bet.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart warns that in a high-uncertainty market being right on the long-term destination can still be fatal, because positioning can be killed several times along a volatile path between here and there.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Argues for path-aware sizing and hedging rather than single-trade conviction on macro destinations.

themes.theme: New Harbor positioning and blow-off risk

insights.claim: New Harbor thinks the market is in a late-stage cycle that may blow off to the upside, with margin debt capable of one more impulse higher before everything comes down hard — a view consistent with McClellan's 2028 margin-debt peak.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Implies participating in the melt-up while planning the exit, rather than fading strength early.

insights.claim: New Harbor is running about 50% equity exposure with no margin, and says it is not trading on its blowoff-top view even though it considers that outcome more likely.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for how a cautious-but-constructive manager is actually positioned into the seasonal turn.

insights.claim: New Harbor's playbook is shape-dependent: a parabolic vertical move toward S&P 8,500-9,000 in weeks would prompt reducing equity into the parabola and possibly buying long-term puts, while a steady 45-degree advance over six months would mean holding around 50% equity and riding the trend.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: A conditional, pre-committed rule set that converts the bullish scenario into specific de-risking triggers and index levels.
insights.quote: We might literally reduce equity into that parabola

insights.claim: New Harbor holds energy stocks, specifically oil service names, purely because they follow the strongest sectors and those have given no reason to sell — an independent confirmation of McClellan's bullish oil call.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Relative-strength money is already positioned long energy, supporting the crude thesis with flows rather than just charts.

insights.claim: Mike Preston flags crude's round trip from about 105 down to 60 and back to 105 as a genuine surprise, underscoring that the bullish oil view has to survive extreme volatility.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Sizing for energy exposure must assume 40%+ drawdowns even within an uptrend.

insights.claim: New Harbor reports a material degradation in its broad stock market indicators and says it is increasingly poised to be on defense — a direct tension with the bullish seasonal call made earlier in the same episode.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: A live divergence between seasonal models and current breadth/trend indicators — worth tracking which resolves first.
insights.quote: we have seen a material degradation in our broad uh stock market indicators

insights.claim: New Harbor's clients widely fear that a Democratic sweep in the midterms would crash the market, and the firm agrees with McClellan that the election outcome does not matter because what matters is predetermined by the cycles and the charts.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Election-hedging demand is likely mispriced; fading midterm-outcome anxiety is the implied trade.

themes.theme: Averages vs. outliers and lost-decade risk

insights.claim: John Lodra argues that averaging cycles destroys the signal that matters for real portfolios, because prolonged negative-return periods are not random events but coincide with conditional factors such as extremely high valuations.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Reframes seasonal composites as poor risk tools even if they are decent timing tools.
insights.quote: we got to kind of concern ourselves not with the average, but the outliers because the outliers aren't random events

insights.claim: Using NASDAQ Dorsey data, a 60/40 portfolio's average cumulative 10-year real return is 87%, but the worst 10-year real return was a loss of about 32% in purchasing power with a drawdown of nearly 41% and roughly 12 years to recover.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the tail that seasonal-average bullishness ignores and argues for inflation-aware allocation rather than passive 60/40.

insights.claim: Citing GMO's lost-decade work and current conditions, New Harbor expects the next decade of 60/40 returns to be very subpar versus average and possibly negative in real terms, even if no top or crash occurs immediately.
insights.speaker: John Lodra (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: A long-horizon warning that coexists with the near-term bullish call — argues for return sources beyond passive beta.

insights.claim: New Harbor's Mike Preston frames the deficit backdrop as having no plan B — stimulus one way or another with the government unable to take its foot off the gas, roughly $40 trillion in debt growing by close to $3 trillion a year, and that is before any recession.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: The fiscal impulse McClellan calls bullish is the same one New Harbor calls the long-term problem — both sides agree it will not stop.

insights.claim: Mike Preston notes the US has not had a real recession since the great financial crisis, discounting the 2020 blip, meaning the record deficits have been run with no cyclical downturn to justify them.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Implies far less fiscal headroom than usual whenever the next genuine recession arrives.

insights.claim: New Harbor is skeptical of McClellan's years-ending-in-seven effect specifically, while agreeing with his presidential-cycle third-year setup and his view that election outcomes do not matter.
insights.speaker: Mike Preston (New Harbor Financial)
insights.so_what: Separates the robust seasonal signal (third year) from the weaker one (decade digit) when weighting the bull case.
